problem_text: A deck of n > 1 cards is given. A positive integer is written on each card. The deck has the property that the arithmetic mean of the numbers on each pair of cards is also the geometric mean of the numbers on some collection of one or more cards. For which n does it follow that the numbers on the cards are all equal?
solution_text: The answer is all n > 1. Proof: Divide all card values by their gcd (the AM-GM property is invariant under scaling since both AM and GM scale linearly), so we may assume the values are coprime (gcd = 1). Let M be the maximum value. If M <= 1, then all values are 1 and we are done. If M >= 2, pick a prime P dividing M. Since gcd = 1, there exists a value not divisible by P; let b be the largest such value. Apply the AM-GM property to the pair (M, b): (M+b)/2 equals the geometric mean of some nonempty collection S. Since (M+b)/2 > b (because M > b), the collection S must contain a value larger than b. By the choice of b, any value larger than b is divisible by P. Hence P divides the product of elements in S. From (M+b)^|S| = 2^|S| * product(S), we get P | (M+b)^|S|. Since P is prime, P | (M+b). But P | M, so P | b, contradicting the choice of b. Therefore M = 1, all values are 1 (in the coprime case), and the original values all equal the gcd d. Thus for all n > 1, the property forces all card values to be equal.
solution_summary: For all n > 1, the property forces all numbers equal. Divide by gcd to reach coprime integers. If the maximum M >= 2, pick a prime P | M and the largest value b not divisible by P. The AM-GM condition on (M, b) forces the geometric-mean collection to contain a value > b, which must be P-divisible, leading to P | b — a contradiction. So M = 1 and all values coincide.
answer: For all n > 1, the property forces all numbers on the cards to be equal (the solution set is {n | 1 < n})

rounds.question: Try n=2: for each pair, the AM equals the GM of some subset. What subsets are possible? What can you conclude? Does this generalize?
rounds.expected_answer: For n=2, subsets can only be {a}, {b}, {a,b}. {a}: (a+b)/2=a implies a=b. {b}: similarly a=b. {a,b}: (a+b)/2=sqrt(ab) implies a=b. n=2 is trivially true, but this method does not generalize to arbitrary n.

rounds.question: Divide all card values by their gcd. Verify that the AM-GM property is preserved under scaling, so we may assume all values are coprime.
rounds.expected_answer: Let d=gcd, g_i=f_i/d. AM: (f_a+f_b)/2 = d*(g_a+g_b)/2. GM: (prod f_i)^(1/k) = d*(prod g_i)^(1/k). Both sides scale by d, so the property is preserved. After division, gcd(g_i)=1.

rounds.question: In the coprime case, let M be the maximum. If M >= 2, pick a prime P | M. Since gcd = 1, there exists a value not divisible by P; let b be the largest such value. Apply the AM-GM property to (M, b) and analyze what the collection S must contain.
rounds.expected_answer: (M+b)/2 > b, so if all values in S were <= b, the GM would be <= b < (M+b)/2, contradiction. So S contains a value > b, which by the choice of b must be divisible by P. Hence P | product(S). From (M+b)^|S| = 2^|S| * product(S), P | (M+b)^|S|, and since P is prime, P | M+b. But P | M, so P | b — contradiction with P ∤ b.

rounds.question: Complete the contradiction chain: from P | product(S) to P | b.
rounds.expected_answer: P | product(S) (since S contains a P-divisible value). (M+b)^k = 2^k * product(S) so P | (M+b)^k. P prime implies P | M+b. P | M implies P | b. But b was chosen so that P ∤ b — contradiction. Therefore M = 1.

rounds.question: Summarize: what does M=1 mean? What are the original values? What is the final answer?
rounds.expected_answer: M=1 and coprime means all g_i = 1, so all f_i = d. Therefore for all n > 1, the property forces all card values to be equal. Answer: all n > 1.
